<reason>Both sides were strong and well-structured, with correct Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 formatting. PRO built a memorable moral frame (the thirty-year library, the seller's free reversion, "defaults are the whole ballgame") and landed a genuinely damaging reframe that contractual claims — leases, policies, plots — are ordinarily heritable, plus a good pressure question about why no heritable tier has appeared despite decades of "license" disclosure. CON, however, converted PRO's own concessions into a decision-shaping dilemma that survived to the end: if the upstream sublicense is personal, PRO's own rule [A4.1] means the button is merely relabeled and nothing transfers, which is CON's remedy; and if it does transfer, PRO conceded the opt-out buyer "may well pay less," which is CON's priced heritable tier with a worse default. CON also anchored this to the motion's operative word "guarantee," which is legitimate engagement with the proposition as written, and answered PRO's market-failure question plausibly by pointing at DRM-free music/game storefronts where rightsholders permit heritability — forcing PRO to narrow its claim to mainstream books and films. CON further kept the privacy default and cross-subsidy objections alive, turning PRO's "windfall not cost" line with the observation that foregone sales are the whole economics of licensing. PRO's best late answer — that voiding non-transferability in anything sold as a "purchase" generates upstream bargaining pressure disclosure cannot — is real and blunts part of the collapse, but it arrives only in closing and is under-developed against CON's standing reply that rightsholders will simply refuse or move to subscriptions. Net: CON made the choice easier to adjudicate.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2 [B4.5] and closing [B5.2]-[B5.4]: using PRO's own answers (storefront "simply cannot call the button 'Buy'" and the opt-out buyer "may well pay less") to show the guarantee either evaporates into honest labeling or becomes CON's priced tier with a more harmful default.</best_rebuttal>
